title: Smoke Inhalation Injury: The Airway Can Worsen After Arrival
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: A patient exposed to smoke in an enclosed-space fire can develop progressive airway edema and toxic inhalation injury even before obvious external burns look severe. Hoarseness, stridor, soot, facial burns, altered mentation, and worsening work of breathing require immediate escalation.
recognize: Enclosed-space exposure, soot around the mouth/nose, singed facial hair, hoarseness, cough, carbonaceous sputum, stridor, confusion, headache, or hypoxemia are concerning cues.
A normal early chest exam does not exclude evolving inhalation injury.
priorities: Escalate early for airway evaluation and advanced airway capability when concerning signs are present.
Use ordered oxygen/monitoring and assess for toxic inhalants such as carbon monoxide according to emergency protocol.
assessMonitor: Trend airway sounds, voice, respiratory effort, mental status, oxygenation, hemodynamics, and exposure history.
interventions: Maintain airway positioning, administer ordered high-concentration oxygen when indicated, and prepare for rapid airway intervention by the appropriate team.
medicationSafety: Do not let a reassuring pulse-oximeter value falsely exclude carbon-monoxide exposure; standard pulse oximetry cannot reliably distinguish carboxyhemoglobin.
teaching: Smoke exposure with breathing difficulty, confusion, syncope, or chest symptoms requires emergency evaluation even when skin burns appear minor.
delegationScope: Airway deterioration requires immediate RN/provider/emergency-team escalation; advanced airway management is outside routine PN/LVN autonomous practice.
examTrap: Waiting for visible airway swelling before escalating a high-risk enclosed-space burn.
oneLinePearl: In smoke injury, the airway may swell after the patient arrives.
sourceBasis: American Burn Association clinical practice and burn-referral guidance

title: Electrical Burns: Small Skin Wounds Can Hide Deep Injury
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Electrical injury may cause deep muscle, cardiac, neurologic, and renal damage that is far greater than the surface wound suggests. High-voltage exposure, arrhythmia, syncope, chest pain, neurologic deficit, or dark urine requires urgent specialty evaluation.
recognize: Entry/exit wounds can be small despite extensive deep-tissue injury.
Dysrhythmia, muscle pain/swelling, weakness, myoglobinuria, falls, or associated trauma may occur.
priorities: Ensure the electrical source is disconnected before contact with the patient.
Escalate for ECG/cardiac, trauma, neurovascular, renal, and burn assessment according to exposure severity.
assessMonitor: Trend rhythm, vital signs, neurovascular status, urine color/output, pain/swelling, and associated trauma.
interventions: Follow burn/trauma protocol and protect affected extremities while specialty evaluation proceeds.
medicationSafety: Analgesia and fluid therapy require ordered monitoring; do not infer fluid needs from surface burn size alone in electrical injury.
teaching: Electrical injuries require medical evaluation because internal injury may not match the skin appearance.
delegationScope: PN/LVN role centers monitoring, ordered care, and escalation; burn/trauma disposition is provider/specialty-team directed.
examTrap: Calling an electrical burn minor because the entry wound is small.

title: Chemical Burns: Stop Exposure Before You Dress the Wound
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
bottomLine: For most chemical skin exposures, immediate removal of contaminated clothing/material and prolonged irrigation after dry-material removal are priorities. Protect staff from secondary contamination and use substance-specific guidance when water is contraindicated.
recognize: Ongoing pain, erythema, tissue discoloration, blistering, powder/residue, or contaminated clothing suggests continued exposure.
priorities: Protect staff, remove the patient from the source, brush off appropriate dry chemicals before irrigation, and follow poison-control/hazard-specific guidance.
Do not delay decontamination for detailed burn-size calculation.
assessMonitor: Assess airway/eyes, exposed body surface, pain, tissue injury, vital signs, and systemic toxicity risk.
interventions: Remove contaminated items and irrigate per chemical-specific protocol; prevent contaminated runoff exposure.
medicationSafety: Do not apply neutralizing chemicals unless specifically directed because exothermic reactions can worsen injury.
teaching: Immediate decontamination and poison-control/emergency guidance are more important than home neutralization attempts.
delegationScope: Hazardous-material procedures require facility PPE/protocol and trained-team coordination.
examTrap: Covering the wound before stopping the chemical exposure.

title: Circumferential Burns: Swelling Can Strangle Perfusion
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Rigid circumferential eschar plus edema can impair distal circulation or chest expansion. Increasing pain, paresthesia, coolness, weak Doppler signals, delayed capillary refill, or ventilatory restriction requires immediate burn-team escalation.
recognize: Distal pulse loss is a late finding; worsening pain, sensory change, tension, coolness, and perfusion changes can appear earlier.
Circumferential chest burns can restrict ventilation as edema increases.
priorities: Perform frequent neurovascular/respiratory checks according to protocol.
Escalate deterioration promptly for burn-surgeon evaluation and possible decompressive therapy.
assessMonitor: Trend pain, color, warmth, sensation, motor function, capillary refill, Doppler/pulses, edema, and respiratory mechanics when chest involved.
interventions: Elevate affected extremities when ordered/appropriate and keep dressings nonconstrictive while awaiting specialty management.
medicationSafety: Analgesia can reduce reported pain but must not substitute for serial perfusion checks.
teaching: New numbness, coolness, severe tightness, or breathing difficulty must be reported immediately.
delegationScope: Serial observations may be performed within role; interpretation of deterioration and escharotomy decisions require immediate specialty escalation.
examTrap: Waiting for absent pulses before reporting a tightening circumferential burn.
oneLinePearl: Pulse loss is late—watch perfusion trends early.

title: Burn Shock: Fluids Are Titrated to Response, Not a Formula Alone
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Major burns cause capillary leak and shock. Resuscitation formulas estimate a starting need, but ongoing fluid therapy must be guided by the burn team's protocol and physiologic response rather than formula volume alone.
recognize: Tachycardia, hypotension, poor perfusion, falling urine output, altered mentation, rising lactate, or excessive edema can signal under- or over-resuscitation.
priorities: Track time of burn, body-weight/TBSA information used by the burn team, urine output, hemodynamics, perfusion, and respiratory status.
Report inadequate response or signs of fluid overload promptly.
assessMonitor: Trend HR/BP, mental status, peripheral perfusion, urine output, edema, lung status, electrolytes, and ordered labs.
interventions: Administer/titrate ordered fluids only within authorized protocol and competency; maintain accurate intake/output.
medicationSafety: Do not independently apply a burn-resuscitation formula as a standing PN/LVN dosing authority.
teaching: Major burn fluid needs change over time and require close hospital monitoring.
delegationScope: Fluid titration authority is protocol/state/facility dependent; PN/LVN role centers accurate monitoring and rapid escalation.
examTrap: Giving the full calculated formula mechanically despite clear signs of overload or poor response.
oneLinePearl: The formula starts the conversation; the patient response guides resuscitation.
sourceBasis: American Burn Association burn-shock resuscitation guideline

title: Major Burns and Hypothermia: Heat Loss Worsens Instability
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
bottomLine: Large burns disrupt skin thermoregulation and expose patients to rapid heat loss during examination, decontamination, transport, and procedures. Preventing hypothermia supports coagulation, perfusion, and recovery.
recognize: Falling core temperature, shivering, cool skin, dysrhythmia, worsening coagulopathy, or hemodynamic instability can accompany hypothermia.
priorities: Minimize unnecessary exposure while completing urgent burn care.
Use warmed environment/blankets/fluids as ordered and monitor core temperature.
assessMonitor: Trend temperature, perfusion, coagulation context, mental status, and warming response.
interventions: Cover unexamined areas, use approved warming devices, and coordinate warming during transport/procedures.
medicationSafety: Avoid direct uncontrolled heat sources that can cause additional burns in patients with impaired sensation.
teaching: Burned skin loses normal temperature protection; warming is part of treatment.
delegationScope: Routine warming/temperature monitoring may be implemented within ordered care; instability requires licensed-team escalation.
examTrap: Leaving a major-burn patient uncovered after the examination because cooling seems secondary to the skin injury.
oneLinePearl: Burned skin loses heat as well as barrier function.

title: Burn Wound Infection: Local Change Plus Systemic Decline Matters
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
bottomLine: Burn wounds are vulnerable to infection, but colonization alone is not the same as invasive infection. New wound deterioration plus fever/hypothermia, hemodynamic change, altered mentation, worsening glucose control, or organ dysfunction requires urgent burn-team evaluation.
recognize: Increasing erythema, purulence, malodor, unexpected wound discoloration, graft loss, increasing pain, or rapid conversion of wound appearance may be concerning when paired with clinical decline.
priorities: Use meticulous infection-prevention technique and trend systemic status.
Escalate suspected invasive infection/sepsis promptly rather than relying on wound appearance alone.
assessMonitor: Monitor wound/graft appearance, temperature, HR/BP, mental status, glucose, urine output, cultures/labs when ordered, and antimicrobial response.
interventions: Perform wound care using prescribed aseptic/clean technique and PPE; obtain cultures only as ordered before antibiotics when clinically feasible without delaying urgent therapy.
medicationSafety: Topical/systemic antimicrobials should be indication-driven; avoid assuming routine prophylactic antibiotics prevent all burn infection.
teaching: After discharge, spreading redness, fever, worsening drainage/odor, or systemic illness requires prompt review.
delegationScope: Routine wound observations may be shared; interpretation of invasive infection/sepsis requires licensed assessment/escalation.
examTrap: Calling a deteriorating patient stable because the burn wound is expected to look abnormal.
oneLinePearl: Burn infection is a wound problem plus a patient problem.
sourceBasis: American Burn Association burn infection/sepsis guidance

title: Burns and Tetanus: Check the Wound and Immunization History
clientNeeds: Health Promotion and Maintenance
Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: CDC classifies burns with devitalized tissue as dirty/major wounds for tetanus risk. Tetanus vaccination and, for selected high-risk patients with incomplete/unknown immunity, tetanus immune globulin are based on wound type and vaccination history—not on giving antibiotics for tetanus prevention.
recognize: Burns, crush injuries, frostbite, and necrotic wounds are examples of dirty/major wounds in CDC tetanus guidance.
priorities: Verify tetanus immunization history and communicate wound classification to the treating team.
Follow current CDC vaccination/TIG recommendations.
assessMonitor: Review vaccine series, last dose, immune status, wound contamination/devitalized tissue, and infection signs.
interventions: Clean/manage the wound and administer ordered vaccination/TIG when indicated.
medicationSafety: CDC does not recommend topical or systemic antibiotics solely to prevent tetanus after a wound.
teaching: Tetanus prevention depends on vaccination history and appropriate wound care; prior tetanus disease does not guarantee immunity.
delegationScope: Vaccination/TIG administration follows order, state law, and facility policy.
examTrap: Choosing prophylactic antibiotics as the primary tetanus-prevention intervention.
oneLinePearl: For tetanus prevention, think wound care + vaccine history ± TIG.
sourceBasis: CDC Clinical Guidance for Wound Management to Prevent Tetanus, June 2025

title: Burn Procedural Pain: Anticipate Dressing-Change Pain
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological Therapies
bottomLine: Burn pain has background, breakthrough, and procedure-related components. Dressing changes and therapy should be anticipated with an individualized analgesia/anxiety plan rather than waiting until severe pain is established.
recognize: Pain may intensify with cleansing, debridement, range-of-motion therapy, or graft/donor-site care.
Fear and prior painful procedures can amplify distress, especially in children.
priorities: Assess pain and anxiety before the procedure and verify the ordered premedication/nonpharmacologic plan.
Monitor respiratory/CNS effects when opioids or sedating adjuncts are used.
assessMonitor: Use age/communication-appropriate pain scale, sedation/respiratory status, response, and functional participation.
interventions: Time ordered analgesia appropriately and use distraction, relaxation, explanation, and trauma-informed support.
medicationSafety: Do not stack sedating medications without reassessing respiratory status and cumulative effect.
teaching: Patients should ask for planned pain control before dressing changes rather than waiting until pain is severe.
delegationScope: Medication administration/monitoring must follow scope and facility policy; sedation decisions are not autonomous PN/LVN functions.
examTrap: Starting an extensive dressing change and planning to medicate only if the patient cannot tolerate it.
oneLinePearl: Burn procedure pain should be planned for, not chased afterward.

title: Burn Rehabilitation: Position and Move Before Contractures Set In
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
Health Promotion and Maintenance
bottomLine: Deep burns and grafted areas can scar into contractures. Positioning, splinting, mobility, and range-of-motion therapy begin early according to burn/rehabilitation plans while protecting grafts and wounds.
recognize: Pain, edema, immobility, wounds across joints, and prolonged flexed positioning increase contracture risk.
priorities: Follow the prescribed anti-contracture positioning, splint, ROM, and mobility plan.
Coordinate analgesia so pain does not unnecessarily prevent therapy.
assessMonitor: Trend joint motion, skin/graft integrity, pain, edema, splint fit, function, and participation.
interventions: Support early mobility/ROM as ordered and protect graft restrictions during healing.
medicationSafety: Analgesia should enable function without causing unsafe oversedation or falls.
teaching: Exercises and positioning may remain important after discharge even when the wound has closed.
delegationScope: Follow PT/OT/burn-team plans; PN/LVN does not independently alter graft precautions or rehabilitation prescriptions.
examTrap: Keeping the burned joint in the most comfortable flexed position all day.
oneLinePearl: Comfort position today can become contracture position tomorrow.
sourceBasis: American Burn Association rehabilitation and early-mobility guidance
